item.passage:
Felix Amaro's name came out of the coffee can on the second Monday of October, which meant that for the next two weeks he would read the morning announcements to all six hundred students of Brookfield Middle School. The announcements were typed on a single sheet and left on the counter in the main office, beside a microphone on a bendable stalk that the secretaries called the goose.

On his first morning Felix read the sheet the way he would have read it to himself, only faster. Lunch would be chicken tacos. The bus for the science fair would leave at noon on Wednesday. Picture retakes were Thursday. He finished in fifty-one seconds, which he knew because he had timed it on the office clock, and he walked back to homeroom feeling that he had done the job well.

Nobody in his homeroom had looked up. Two girls had been finishing math homework through the whole thing, and when the bus to the science fair left at noon on Wednesday, three people missed it.

On Thursday morning Mrs. Daly, the head secretary, watched him pull the goose toward his mouth. "Who are you talking to?" she asked.

"Everybody," Felix said.

"That's the trouble. Nobody listens to everybody." She tapped the sheet. "Pick one person. Somebody who actually needs to know this stuff. Read it to them."

Felix thought about it while the bell rang. He did not know who needed to hear about picture retakes. Then he thought of Mr. Reyes, the custodian, whom he had seen that week in the boiler room off the gym, eating a sandwich beside a gray speaker bolted to the wall. The speaker was the only thing in the room besides the furnace and Mr. Reyes. Every word Felix said went there, to one man with a sandwich.

So he read the sheet to Mr. Reyes. He slowed down for the times. He paused after "picture retakes," the way you pause when you are telling someone a thing that might matter to them, and he said "Thursday, that's today" instead of only "Thursday." When he got to the end, he said, "That's all, have a good day," and for once he meant it as a sentence and not as a noise.

It took three minutes and ten seconds. Mrs. Daly said nothing, but she nodded at the clock.

At lunch a boy he barely knew asked whether the retakes were really today. That afternoon, passing the gym, Felix saw Mr. Reyes leaning on a mop in the doorway of the boiler room.

"Retakes are Thursday," Mr. Reyes said. "That's today." He said it in Felix's voice, slow, with the pause in the middle, and then he grinned and went back to the floor.

Someone has put it on the fence post
at the corner of Alder and Third,
a child's red mitten, thumb up,
the way you would set a cup on a shelf

so its owner could find it. It has been there
since the first snow, eleven days now.
Each morning I pass it on the way to work
and each morning it is a little different:

a cap of new snow, then none,
then a crust of ice along the cuff
from the sleet on Tuesday, then the thumb
bent over as if it had given up waving.

I have asked around about whose it is.
The mail carrier says it was there before her route.
The crossing guard says she watches the post,
but children look at their feet, never up.

I keep thinking of the other one,
the left mitten, at home in a coat pocket,
or worn alone on one cold hand,
its owner holding the bare one in a sleeve.

It is a small thing, a found thing,
held up where anyone could see it,
and what moves me is the stranger
who stopped in the cold to put it there,

who did not know the child either
and did it anyway, on the chance,
which is how most of the good
in the world arrives, I think: on the chance.

My father had meant to teach me to change a tire in our driveway, on a dry Saturday, with a thermos of coffee on the hood. Instead I learned on the shoulder of County Road 12 in a cold drizzle, at seventeen, with trucks going by close enough to rock the car.

We had been driving back from my aunt's when the steering began to pull, and then there was a flapping sound from the right rear, like a flag in wind. My father guided us onto the gravel and switched on the hazard lights. Then, instead of getting out, he handed me the keys. "Your car someday," he said. "Your tire today."

The spare was under the floor of the trunk, beneath a panel I had never known could lift.

He did not touch a single tool. He stood beside me in his windbreaker and talked. Loosen the lug nuts first, while the tire is still on the ground, or the wheel will only spin. Turn them a half turn each and stop. Find the notch under the frame for the jack; there is one behind or ahead of each wheel, and the manual will show it. Raise the car until the flat tire just clears the gravel.

My hands were wet and the lug wrench kept slipping. On the fourth nut I put my whole weight on the handle and nothing happened, and then something did, all at once, and I nearly went down in the gravel. My father said, "Righty-tighty, lefty-loosey," which I had heard my whole life and had always thought was a joke.

When the spare was on, he made me tighten the nuts in a star pattern, across from one another rather than around the circle, so the wheel would sit evenly. Then he made me lower the car and tighten them again, harder, now that the tire could no longer turn in the air.

The whole thing took me forty minutes. I am told a good mechanic can do it in five. When we were back in the car, my father wrote the date on a scrap of paper and put it in the glove box. I asked him what it was for. He said it was so that the next time I had a flat, alone, I would remember that I had already done it once in the rain, and that the rain had been the hard part.

In 1895 Corvell Falls, a mill town of about eleven thousand people on the Ashby River, had running water in roughly one house in five. The rest drew water from yard pumps or bought it by the barrel, and a bath, for most of the families who worked in the town's three woolen mills, meant a tin tub filled from the kettle on Saturday night, the whole family taking turns in the same water.

The town's physician, Dr. Helen Marsh, had argued for years that this was a matter of health as much as comfort. Skin infections spread through the mill boardinghouses every summer, and lice through the schools every fall. In the spring of 1895 she proposed that the town build a public bathhouse on Canal Street, where any resident could have a hot shower, soap, and a clean towel for one cent.

The proposal drew two objections. The first was cost: the building, its boiler, and its piping were estimated at nine thousand dollars, a large sum for a town that had only recently paved its main street. The second was harder to answer. Several members of the council believed that workers would refuse to bathe in public, and that the town would be left with an expensive, empty building. One councilman said that a man's bath was his own business.

Dr. Marsh answered the second objection with a count. With the owners' permission, she stationed a clerk at the gate of the largest mill for a week and had him ask every worker leaving the evening shift a single question: would you pay a penny for a hot shower on your way home? Of the 812 workers asked, 641 said yes.

The council approved the bathhouse that summer, by one vote. It opened in October of 1896 with twenty-four shower stalls, twelve for men and twelve for women, each with a door that locked from the inside. On its first Saturday it gave 1,140 showers, and the attendant ran out of towels by three in the afternoon and sent a boy to borrow more from the hotel.

The councilman who had called bathing a private matter was seen in the line the following week. When a reporter from the Corvell Falls Ledger asked him about it, he said that the stall had a door, and that what a man did behind a locked door was still his own business.

choices: Onions developed strong flavors mainly to attract animals that spread their seeds.

item.passage:
An onion sitting whole on the counter will not make anyone cry. You can hold it, peel off its papery skin, even sniff it, and your eyes will stay dry. The trouble begins with the knife, and the reason lies in a chemical trap that the onion sets for anything that bites it.

Inside each onion cell, two sets of ingredients are kept apart. One is a group of sulfur-containing compounds. The other is an enzyme, a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction, stored in a separate compartment of the cell. As long as the cell is whole, the two stay apart and nothing happens.

Cutting tears cells open and lets the enzyme reach the sulfur compounds. Within seconds a chain of reactions begins. The enzyme breaks the compounds into new substances, and one of these is quickly turned, with the help of a second enzyme, into a gas called syn-propanethial-S-oxide. Chemists call it the lachrymatory factor, from the Latin word for tears.

The gas drifts up from the cutting board and reaches the surface of the eye, where it stimulates nerve endings that signal a sting. The body responds the way it responds to dust or smoke: the eyes produce tears to flush the irritant away. The more cells a cut breaks open, the more gas is released, which is one reason a dull knife, which crushes as much as it slices, tends to produce more tears than a sharp one.

Scientists generally think the system evolved as a defense. An animal that takes a bite of a wild onion gets a mouthful of harsh, irritating chemicals, and it may learn to leave the next onion alone. The same reactions also produce many of the sharp flavors cooks prize in a raw onion. Heat destroys the enzymes, which is why a cooked onion tastes mild and sweet, and why onions already softening in a pan rarely bring tears.

Kitchen advice for avoiding tears follows directly from the chemistry. Chilling an onion before cutting slows the reactions and keeps the gas from rising as quickly. A sharp knife breaks fewer cells. Some cooks work near a fan or an open window to carry the gas away before it reaches their eyes. None of these methods stops the reaction entirely; they only reduce how much of the gas finds its way to the eye.
